Property advertising on Facebook and Instagram: how to generate quality leads

How to build a systematic approach to real estate lead generation with Meta Ads in 2026.

When a real estate agency or developer launches Facebook and Instagram advertising, the expectation is usually straightforward: allocate a budget, define an audience and start receiving enquiries from prospective buyers.

In practice, Meta Ads is more complicated.

The platform does not know exactly who is ready to buy a home today. It cannot guarantee a particular number of leads, let alone that everyone who leaves their details is ready to attend a viewing and pay a deposit immediately.

The first thing an advertiser competes for on Meta is attention.

A prospective property buyer encounters dozens of other offers at the same time: other residential developments, agencies, independent agents and developers. Property advertising also competes with everything else in that person's feed.

Effective lead generation therefore starts with a system that attracts the right audience's attention, tests several reasons to take an interest and gradually identifies which ones resonate with the market. Searching for a single “perfect setting” that delivers a ready-to-buy customer will not achieve this.

This is the key distinction between simply setting up ads and building a systematic lead generation process.

01

Why getting the Meta Ads settings right is only part of the work

One of the most common questions when launching property advertising is how precisely the audience can be targeted.

The reasoning is understandable: define a prospective buyer's age, location, interests and other characteristics as accurately as possible, and the ads should reach people more likely to buy.

However, potential reach and actual demand are very different things.

An estimated audience of a million people does not represent a million prospective buyers. It includes people with different incomes, personal circumstances and levels of readiness to consider a property purchase right now.

Other advertisers are also competing within that audience. In a large city, dozens of agencies, developers and individual listings may compete for one prospective customer's attention.

Narrowing the audience further does not solve this on its own.

At RESET, we usually start with relatively broad audiences and put much of the work into what people see in the ad and which offer they respond to.

This is where the creative becomes central.

A strong property ad needs more than an attractive development render, a logo and a “Learn more” button. Within a few moments, it must give someone a clear reason to stop and consider this particular offer.

Before launching, we break the product down into its individual selling points.

A development under construction might have several strengths: a 10% down payment, an extended instalment plan, a particular apartment price, a finished interior, a location near the sea or a limited number of homes at a special price.

Trying to give all these benefits equal prominence in one message is a mistake.

At RESET, we use a creative principle we call “The Arrow”.

Every ad needs one primary message: the reason someone will stop scrolling. The other elements support and explain it without competing for attention.

If a 10% down payment is the main offer, it becomes the central message. Price, floor area, neighbourhood, instalment period and other details sit further down the information hierarchy.

This turns a list of property features into a specific offer.

Even a well-chosen audience and strong creative cannot guarantee results in advance.

That brings us to the most important part of our method: we develop several hypotheses and let the market reveal which offer performs best.

02

Why we test offers before choosing a winner

A common mistake in property advertising is selecting a single offer that “should work” before the campaign has even launched.

Imagine an agency selling several properties: one at the more affordable end of the market, another in the middle segment and a third in the premium segment. Each has its own price, purchase terms, location and benefits.

It is possible to select one strong offer for each property, produce good creative and launch all three under the same conditions.

Yet the results might look like this: leads for the first property cost $5, leads for the second cost $12, and the third spends budget while generating almost no enquiries.

The first reaction is often predictable: the creative is weak, the audience is wrong or the specialist made a setup mistake.

That is not always the explanation.

Advertising operates in a changing market. Demand shifts, competitors launch their own offers, some purchase terms become more attractive than others, and audience interest is uneven.

We have even seen two branches of the same company use almost identical advertising materials and get different results.

The specialist's job is to design a test that reveals which offers deserve more budget and which do not. No one can reliably predict every winner in advance.

This is why RESET does not build a campaign launch around a single hypothesis.

If a property offers several reasons to buy, we treat them as separate advertising angles: the down payment, apartment price, instalment plan, completion status, interior finish, location or another competitive advantage.

These are different reasons to take an interest in the property, rather than ten design variations of the same banner.

Suppose we begin with ten advertising angles.

The first data shows a weak audience response to some of them. We pause or rework those angles, leaving seven.

More data allows us to remove further combinations that underperform.

We then concentrate the budget on three or four approaches that the market has validated, instead of continuing to spread it across every initial idea.

RESET creates competition between hypotheses and gradually moves budget towards the ones that win.

03

Why the cheapest lead is not our objective

Once a campaign launches, cost per lead often becomes the main measure used to judge Meta Ads.

For example, one campaign generates enquiries at $3, another at $7 and a third at $15.

The first may appear to be outperforming the third. Cost per lead alone, however, cannot establish that.

Across RESET campaigns, we have generated enquiries at very different prices. That is normal: cost depends on the property, offer, audience, competition, campaign period and many other factors.

A more important distinction is the business value of those leads: a $3 lead and a $15 lead can have very different potential.

Meta optimises towards the action we specify. If the only objective is to maximise the number of forms completed at the lowest possible cost, its algorithm will seek out people who complete that action most cheaply.

A cheap form submission does not necessarily represent a prospective buyer.

This is especially noticeable with very simple lead forms. Someone sees an ad, taps a button, confirms automatically filled contact details and submits. Reducing the number of steps can increase enquiry volume, but it can also increase accidental submissions.

Sales teams recognise the consequences: people do not answer the phone, say they never submitted a form, only wanted to browse or cannot remember the ad at all.

The lead form is therefore part of the qualification process.

A few additional questions may raise the cost per enquiry while filtering out some accidental submissions and giving the sales representative useful information before the first conversation.

The aim is to strike a balance. A twenty-question form will put off some genuine prospective buyers.

This is why we look beyond CPL when evaluating a campaign. We want an economically viable enquiry cost and leads that the sales team can work with.

That distinction matters.

An advertising dashboard can look impressive with a very low cost per lead. If most of those people never get past the first attempt at contact, the result means little to the business.

The next question is more useful: what quality of lead can Meta Ads deliver, and what should happen after an enquiry arrives?

04

What quality of lead should you expect from Meta Ads?

It helps to understand how the channel works.

Someone searching Google for “buy a two-room apartment in Odesa” is actively looking for an offer. On Meta, the situation is different.

A person scrolling through Instagram or Facebook, watching Stories or Reels, or reading posts encounters a property ad. They may not have been looking for a home that day at all.

The ad's role is to attract their attention, present a relevant offer and turn potential interest into an action.

Expecting every Meta lead to have already chosen a home and be ready to arrive with the money tomorrow is unrealistic.

That does not make the lead poor.

Property purchases rarely follow a single interaction. Weeks or months can pass between initial interest and a completed deal.

Someone may enquire, check the instalment terms, compare other properties, speak to a representative, return to the question later and only then decide.

Lead generation therefore continues beyond the form submission.

The next stages of the funnel are:

enquiry → contact → qualification → meeting/viewing → deal.

Judging marketing only by the first stage can lead to the wrong conclusions.

One campaign may produce many cheap enquiries, of which few qualify. Another may deliver fewer, more expensive enquiries, but representatives reach more of those people, arrange meetings and move them further through the funnel.

The second campaign may be considerably more valuable to the business.

Sales feedback is therefore an extension of our advertising analysis.

We need to understand what happens after each enquiry: whether the team reaches the person, whether their needs match the offer, whether a meeting or viewing takes place, and whether they continue towards a deal.

Meta creates a flow of opportunities for the sales team. The quality of the overall system depends on how well marketing and sales work together to develop them.

05

Why a campaign needs ongoing management

Even a successful combination of audience, offer and creative will not work forever.

People gradually interact with the advertising. Some have already seen the offer, some have enquired, and others have scrolled past several times and stopped responding. Meanwhile, competitors and their offers change, as does the market's response.

A campaign therefore needs ongoing management.

At RESET, some combinations remain effective for several weeks or longer, while others lose momentum much sooner. We do not refresh ads simply because a fixed number of days has passed.

We follow the data.

Rising enquiry costs, falling lead volume or changes in quality reported by the sales team tell us it is time to revisit the hypotheses.

We might refresh certain creatives, find a new angle for a strong property, test another offer or introduce a new advertising approach.

Meta Ads becomes a continuous cycle:

hypotheses → launch → data → selection → scaling → feedback → new hypotheses.

Launching a campaign is the beginning of the work.

A strong campaign relies on a system that continually finds effective combinations and replaces them as the market changes.

06

What determines Meta Ads results in real estate?

There is no setting in Meta Ads that selects only people ready to buy property immediately.

No creative can be guaranteed to win before it runs.

And the lowest cost per enquiry does not necessarily deliver the best business result.

RESET builds its lead generation process around these realities.

We break down the offer, identify reasons to buy, develop advertising hypotheses around them, test the market's response and gradually concentrate budget on the approaches that perform best.

After launch, we assess enquiry quality and sales feedback alongside the advertising dashboard.

Our objective is a manageable flow of prospective buyers at a cost that allows the business to work with them and convert a proportion into deals.

This is what systematic lead generation with Meta Ads means to us.
